conbody.p: Copyright is an issue that most Americans interact with in one way or another at some point in their lives. Intellectual property surrounds us, acting as a necessary ingredient in the melting pot that is popular culture. The right to create and capitalize on your creation is a fundamentally American principle. While copyright law can be rather costly and difficult to litigate, it has been proven that in being so, the power balance between the holder and the consumer is kept. Without this lengthy process, and especially in the era of the internet, holders are prone to acting in predatory ways, “trolling” for infringers as way to gain a secondary stream of income. While other abuses of copyright have come to light like police officers relying on Digital Millenium Copyright Act (DMCA) takedown notices to avoid being videotaped, most if not all return to overreaches in authority and greed.

Passed in December of 2020, the Copyright Alternative in Small-Claims Enforcement (CASE) Act, brings this power balance—the only safeguard against exploitation of the consumer—under threat. The CASE Act seeks to expedite the process of copyright litigation, lowering the cost for the holder to file suit, while supposedly lowering the monetary stakes for the infringer. While at first glance this change may seem ideal for both parties, it increases the likelihood of predatory acts, as the difficulty of litigating copyright law becomes far less complicated. In the digital era, copyright infringement has become incredibly easy to carry out. With current proof of infringement guidelines still in place, whether accidental or intentional, one can be slapped with life-ruining fines. Simply put, the punishment must match the crime. Moreover, the consumer must be protected from the big players who seek only to use infringement for exploitative purposes, seeking to protect only their pocketbooks and not the integrity of their work.
